summary.text: 武 means “military” or “martial.” It combines 戈, a weapon, with 止, originally a foot sign. Read as armed movement, the pair suggests a force setting out on campaign. The famous idea of “stopping weapons” is a later interpretation of the same visible parts.

formation.text: Pictures of a weapon and a foot combine to convey armed movement. Both are form components: the objects they depict contribute to the scene.

components.text: The upper and right-hand strokes descend from a picture of a long-handled weapon. Its shape has changed in clerical and regular writing, so it no longer matches a separately written 戈 exactly.
止 depicts a foot, supplying the image of advancing. Its role follows the depicted object, not the modern word meaning “stop.”

history.text: The combination is already present in oracle writing. Bronze inscriptions use 武 for military affairs and martial strength. This gives the armed-movement interpretation support beyond a convenient explanation of the modern shape.

The modern strokes preserve an altered version of this early combination. The weapon part no longer has the standalone outline of 戈. This change of shape should be distinguished from replacing the weapon with a different meaningful component.

The traditional “stop the weapons” reading interprets martial achievement as ending war. It is an important interpretation of the character’s meaning, but does not by itself establish why its earliest form was created.

uncertainties.text: The expedition scene is an interpretation of the weapon and foot combination. Early 止 often denotes movement, which makes that reading preferable to treating its familiar meaning “stop” as automatic proof of the original design.
